title: "A clear victory"
hook: the treaty is called a clear victory, and peace lets the call of Islam spread (48:1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the treaty at Hudaybiyyah, a peace that hurt. Your line was it looked like losing. What did you let go of for the sake of peace? Day two hundred seventy-four.

The pilgrims are riding home to Medina, heads shaved, no pilgrimage done, and the mood is heavy. Umar can't let it go. He rides up beside the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and asks him something, and gets no answer. He asks again. No answer. A third time. Nothing. Umar drops back, sure he's gone too far, afraid a verse is about to come down about him. Then someone calls his name: the Prophet wants you. Umar rides up, braced for the worst. And the Prophet says, as Sahih al-Bukhari tells it: tonight a surah has come to me that is dearer to me than everything the sun rises on. Today: a clear victory.
screen: `RIDING HOME, HEADS SHAVED.` → `UMAR ASKS THREE TIMES.` → `DEARER THAN ALL THE SUN RISES ON.`

segments.voice: The surah is al-Fath, the Victory, Surah 48. And it opens: we have given you a clear victory, fathan mubina. Fath means an opening, and a victory. It's the same root as al-Fattah, the Opener, one of the names we met a few weeks ago. Umar, in another report, asks the obvious thing: messenger of God, is this a victory? And the Prophet says: yes. Everyone could see what had been lost. What the surah saw was what had been opened. Here's how it played out. With the roads at peace, people could travel between Mecca and Medina without fear. They talked. They traded. Families on both sides met again. And they heard the Qur'an, not over the noise of war, but in ordinary conversation. The early scholar az-Zuhri, as Ibn Ishaq reports him, said there was no greater victory in Islam before it: in the two years after Hudaybiyyah, as many people became Muslim as in all the years before, or more. Ibn Hisham, who edited Ibn Ishaq's book, pointed to the numbers: about fourteen hundred came to Hudaybiyyah, and two years later, ten thousand marched to Mecca. Two of Mecca's commanders, Khalid ibn al-Walid, the man who turned the battle at Uhud, and 'Amr ibn al-'As, both came to Medina during the peace and became Muslim. Even the clause that hurt most, sending back those who fled Mecca, was dropped by the Meccans themselves not long after, when it started to cost them more than it cost the Muslims. The Qur'an says elsewhere that you may dislike something that is good for you. Hudaybiyyah is often told to show what that line means.
screen: `FATH — AN OPENING, A VICTORY.` · `IS THIS A VICTORY? YES.` · `FOURTEEN HUNDRED, THEN TEN THOUSAND.` · `YOU MAY DISLIKE WHAT IS GOOD.` · then, large: `LOSING, THEN WINNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look again at a setback. Sit, and bring back something from your past that felt like a clear loss at the time. The rejection. The breakup. The plan that fell apart. Stay with how it felt then. Now look at what it opened. What came into your life through the gap it left? It may be nothing yet. That's allowed. Just look, with the question Umar asked: is this a victory? The bell holds the time.
A clear victory. Fathan mubina: what the Qur'an called the treaty everyone thought was a loss, the peace that opened the way. Today's word.
Your line: losing, then winning. Today, when something goes against you, say to yourself: it's too early to call it. Day two hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Some Muslims recite Surah al-Fath in times of hope, and teachers point to Hudaybiyyah when counseling patience with setbacks and trust that a loss may be an opening.

fork.setup: you're Umar, riding home from Hudaybiyyah. the Prophet tells you a surah has come calling this a clear victory. what do you ask?
options: nothing. you accept it at once.
messenger of God, is this a victory?
can we go back and fight?
fork.reveal: he asked the obvious thing, and the Prophet answered: yes. what everyone saw lost, the surah saw opened.

original.note: Arabic: a clear victory, a clear opening (48:1). fath shares a root with al-Fattah, the Opener.

trapdoor: what you thought: a victory in battle.
what it means: a treaty that looked like losing, called a clear victory, because peace opened the way for the call of Islam.
what a scholar hears: fath means opening before it means conquest; az-Zuhri's judgment on Hudaybiyyah is preserved by Ibn Ishaq.

sources.ref: Qur'an 48:1 (we have given you a clear victory)

Sahih Muslim 1785 (is it a victory? yes)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (via Ibn Hisham): az-Zuhri on the victory; Ibn Hisham's comparison of 1,400 and 10,000; the conversions of Khalid and 'Amr
Qur'an 2:216 (you may dislike a thing that is good for you)

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: 'with ten years of peace' implied the truce lasted ten years (it broke within two, as day 277 tells), now 'with the roads at peace'; the 1,400-to-10,000 comparison attributed to Ibn Hisham and az-Zuhri's judgment to Ibn Ishaq; cut 'best commanders' and 'the story Muslims tell'; howItsDone no longer claims a common recitation custom.
The index hook says 'the message spread'; the validator flags 'the message' as a translation name, so the hook field reads 'the call of Islam spread'. Consider rewording the outline line.
Pickthall renders 48:1 as 'a signal victory'; the script uses the index's 'a clear victory' and doesn't claim Pickthall's wording. Confirm.
Some commentators read 'victory' in 48:1 as the later conquest of Mecca or of Khaybar; the script follows the view (with Umar's hadith) that it's Hudaybiyyah itself.
The dropping of the return clause after Abu Basir's band (Bukhari 2731) is summarized without naming Abu Basir.
